CHAPTER 11: NATIONAL INCOME

INTRODUCTION - KEY DEFINITIONS
- National income: the income going to the permanent residents of a country from current (continuous) economic activity during a period of time, usually one year.
- Economic activity: producing, distributing, buying, selling and working.
- National income gives an idea of how wealthy a country is.
- A rise in national income can show the economy has grown and the nation is wealthier.
- Recession: a fall in gross domestic product (GDP) in two successive quarters (two three-month periods).
- Quarter: a period of three months.

THE CIRCULAR FLOW OF INCOME
- Circular flow of income: shows the flow of money in the economy between households, firms, the government, financial institutions and foreign markets. Money flows round in an endless loop.
- Diagram in words (Figure 11.1): Households are on one side, firms on the other.
  - Households supply factors of production (e.g. labour) to firms.
  - Firms pay households incomes for these factors (e.g. wages).
  - Households spend some of their income on the output of firms.
  - Leakages flow out: taxes go to the GOVERNMENT, savings go to FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, imports go to FOREIGN MARKETS.
  - Injections flow back in: government expenditure from the government, investment from financial institutions, exports from foreign markets.
- Not all household income is spent on the output of firms, because of leakages.

LEAKAGES (reduce aggregate demand)
- 1. Taxes: households pay part of their income to the government.
- 2. Savings: households save part of their income in financial institutions.
- 3. Imports: households spend some income on goods from abroad, e.g. an Irish person buying a car made in Germany adds to Germany's national income.

INJECTIONS (increase aggregate demand)
- 1. Government expenditure: the government spends money on the output of firms.
- 2. Investment: financial institutions lend money back into the economy, e.g. to entrepreneurs opening a business.
- 3. Exports: firms get money from foreign consumers, e.g. a German buying Irish-made medicine adds to Ireland's national income.

RULE
- Injections increase national income; leakages reduce it.
- If injections are greater than leakages, national income rises.
- If injections are less than leakages, national income falls.

MEASURING NATIONAL INCOME
- The Central Statistics Office (CSO) compiles national income data in Ireland.
- Three methods. The CSO mainly uses methods 1 and 3, and produces an estimate for method 2.
- Method 1, Expenditure method: total money spent on final goods and services in the year. Y = C + I + G + (X - M).
  - Y = national income, C = consumption, I = investment, G = government spending, X = exports, M = imports.
  - X - M can be written NX = net exports.
- Method 2, Output method: add the output figures of all firms in the economy.
  - Must avoid double counting: this happens if spending on intermediate goods is included.
  - Example: a farmer sells potatoes to a fast food restaurant for 200 euro. The restaurant makes chips worth 500 euro. The value of output is 500 euro, NOT 700 euro (farmer's 200 euro plus 300 euro value added).
- Method 3, Income method: add incomes paid to those supplying factors of production. The CSO includes profits of companies and the self-employed, remuneration (pay) of employees, and rent of dwellings.
  - Transfer payments are NOT included. Transfer payment: a payment for which no factor of production has been supplied, e.g. social welfare such as child benefit.
  - Secondary benefits ARE included, e.g. the value of a company car or health insurance paid by the employer.
- The three methods check each other and should give similar results.

THE EXPENDITURE METHOD IN DETAIL
C: Consumption expenditure depends on:
- Incomes: higher wages mean higher disposable income and more spending.
- Direct taxes: a cut in taxes on labour raises disposable income and spending.
- Consumer sentiment/confidence: if a downturn is expected, spending falls today.
- The marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
- Interest rates: high rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, so spending falls.
- Availability of credit: more bank lending means more consumption.
I: Investment
- Investment: capital formation, i.e. making capital goods, e.g. building a factory or expanding a business premises. Office construction is an example.
- Depends on: business expectations (optimism raises investment); interest rates (funds are often borrowed, so low rates mean more investment); taxes (a rise in corporation tax would reduce investment in Ireland by MNCs).
G: Government spending
- Example of current spending: paying public sector salaries.
- Depends on: current revenue from taxation; the ability of the NTMA (National Treasury Management Agency) to borrow money (sell bonds) at low interest rates; EU rules - deficit should not exceed 3% of GDP and public debt must be below 60% of GDP (rules relaxed during Covid-19).
X: Exports
- Examples: Irish beef and butter sold abroad (goods); foreign tourists visiting Ireland (services).
- Depend on: incomes abroad (higher foreign incomes raise demand for Irish exports); exchange rates (a fall in the value of the euro makes Irish exports more attractive outside the eurozone and boosts tourism from non-eurozone countries).
- Class activity: euro moving from 1.20 dollars to 1.10 dollars (euro weaker) makes Irish exports cheaper in the US; euro moving to 1.30 dollars (euro stronger) makes them dearer.
M: Imports
- Examples: cars and bananas (goods); Irish tourists going abroad (services).
- Depend on: incomes in Ireland (higher incomes raise demand for German cars); marginal propensity to import (MPM); exchange rates (a weaker euro makes imports from outside the eurozone dearer and less attractive).

WORKED EXAMPLE
- C = 2,500m, I = 500m, G = 600m, X = 300m, M = 200m.
- Y = 2,500 + 500 + 600 + (300 - 200) = 3,700m euro.

REASONS FOR CALCULATING NATIONAL INCOME
- 1. Measure economic growth: e.g. 100 billion in Year 1 and 105 billion in Year 2 = 5% growth. Shows performance over time.
- 2. Economic planning: helps policymakers decide, e.g. cut direct taxes on labour, then check if the cut raised national income.
- 3. Standard of living: shows whether economic activity, and so living standards, rose or fell. Irish GDP fell 2008-2012 after the financial crash and rose from 2013 to 2020.
- 4. Indebtedness: debt is compared to national income (debt/GDP ratio). This ratio can affect interest rates (bond yields) on government borrowing.
  - Country A: debt 90bn, GDP 100bn, ratio 90%. Country B: debt 90bn, GDP 200bn, ratio 45%. Country B is less indebted, more attractive to lend to, so may pay lower interest rates.
- 5. EU budget contribution: a member state's contribution is based on its gross national income (GNI).

LIMITATIONS OF NATIONAL INCOME STATISTICS
Example: GDP Year 1 = 10bn, Year 2 = 20bn (looks like a 100% rise).
- 1. Population: if the population doubled from 1 million to 2 million, GDP per capita (GDP / population) is unchanged at 10,000 euro.
- 2. Nature of goods produced: if 12bn of the rise is military spending (e.g. weapons) instead of food and healthcare, people may be worse off. North Korea puts big resources into its military at the expense of consumer goods.
- 3. Inflation/deflation: 10 billion items at 1 euro, then 10 billion items at 2 euro - the rise is all price, not output. The CSO uses constant prices (e.g. valuing 2021 and 2022 output at 2020 prices).
  - Nominal GDP: GDP valued at current prices.
  - Real GDP: GDP valued at constant prices. A change in real GDP can only come from a change in quantity produced.
- 4. Distribution of wealth: GDP does not show how income is shared; extra wealth may go to a few rich people. The Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI) can help (Chapter 16).
- 5. Unpaid work is not counted, e.g. GAA volunteers, charity workers, stay-at-home parents.
- 6. GDP per capita is an average; many people earn much less or much more than the average.
- 7. Welfare/wellbeing is not shown: higher GDP may come with longer hours, longer commutes, more workload and stress.
- 8. The hidden/shadow economy is not counted.

THE HIDDEN (SHADOW) ECONOMY
- Hidden/shadow economy: unrecorded economic activity not counted in national income statistics.
- Examples: illegal drugs trade, fuel laundering, cigarette smuggling, people dealing in cash who do not submit tax returns.
Impact on the economy and society:
- Lower sales and profits for legitimate retailers: a shop selling cigarettes at 14 euro competes with a smuggler at 5 euro.
- Higher unemployment if legitimate firms lose sales; this means less tax revenue and more jobseeker's allowance costs.
- Less government revenue: VAT and excise duties are not collected, so less money for current spending.
- Scarce resources spent fighting it (customs at ports, Garda investigations, prisons). Opportunity cost: e.g. fewer Gardaí for community policing or road safety checkpoints.
- Health and safety: counterfeit alcohol, cigarettes and perfume follow no safety rules and may harm health.
How the government can reduce it:
- Harsher fines and prison sentences.
- More resources for Gardaí and customs.
- More funding for awareness campaigns about dangers of hidden-economy goods.
- Lower indirect taxes, removing the incentive to buy in the hidden economy.
- Lower taxes on labour, reducing the incentive to work for cash to avoid USC, PAYE and PRSI.

INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY (IP)
- Intellectual property: patents, trademarks, copyrights and trade secrets.
- Patent: gives the inventor the sole right to produce their invention.
- Trademark: brand names, e.g. Coca-Cola, McDonald's.
- Copyright: applies to creative works, e.g. books, music, films.
- Trade secret: a process not known outside the company, e.g. a recipe or production method.
- Foreign MNCs have located IP in their Irish operations for tax reasons. IP earnings flowing into Ireland boost national income figures; profits sent back (repatriated) to the MNC's home country reduce national income. This distorts Ireland's data.
- Example - Tasty Cakes: IP (secret recipe) registered to the Irish HQ. Tasty Cakes France sells 100m of cakes and pays 90m to the Irish HQ for use of the recipe and trademark. The Irish HQ is very profitable; the French firm is not. The firm avoids the higher French corporation tax and pays the Irish rate (12.5%). Firms doing this have been accused of tax avoidance.
- Many MNCs (pharmaceutical and big tech firms) hold IP in Ireland; this inflates Ireland's national income statistics.

THE 2015 GDP SURGE
- In 2016 the CSO revised Ireland's 2015 GDP up to 260bn: 26% growth on 2014 (208bn). This drew international criticism.
- Reasons:
  - 1. Relocation of IP by MNCs to Ireland, so their international IP earnings were recorded in Irish GDP.
  - 2. Inversion deals: a firm with an Irish HQ takes over or merges with a foreign firm and the new firm's earnings appear as Irish. E.g. Medtronic (large US medical device firm) merged with Covidien, which had its HQ in Ireland; the merged firm's HQ was in Ireland.
  - 3. Aircraft leasing companies moved billions of euro of assets to Ireland.
- Result: GDP was clearly not a suitable measure of the standard of living in Ireland.

GDP AND GNP
- GDP (gross domestic product): value of goods and services produced by Irish- AND foreign-owned factors of production in the domestic economy only.
- GNP (gross national product): value of goods and services produced by Irish-owned factors of production in the domestic economy AND abroad.
- GDP is used internationally, but in Ireland it does not reflect domestic performance well; GNP has long been seen as better for Ireland's standard of living.
- GDP + net factor income from the rest of the world = GNP.
- Net factor income from the rest of the world (NFYFROW) = income earned by Irish factors abroad sent to Ireland MINUS income earned by foreign factors in Ireland sent abroad.
- Income earned by Irish factors abroad: profits of Irish firms abroad (e.g. Bank of Ireland's UK subsidiary); emigrants' remittances (e.g. an Irish nurse in Australia sending money home); interest earned by Irish bondholders on foreign debt.
- Income earned by foreign factors in Ireland: profits of foreign MNCs in Ireland (e.g. Apple, Boston Scientific, Facebook); immigrants' remittances (e.g. an American programmer at Google's Irish HQ sending money home); interest on Irish debt held by foreign bondholders.
- In Ireland NFYFROW is negative because there are more foreign MNCs repatriating profits, more foreign workers sending money home, and more non-residents earning interest on Irish debt. So Irish GNP is smaller than GDP.
- 2019 (preliminary): GDP 356,051m; NFYFROW -81,721m; GNP 274,330m.

GNI AND GNDI
- GNI (gross national income): total income earned by a country's residents and businesses, wherever it is earned. It measures income, not output.
  - GNP + EU subsidies - EU taxes = GNI.
  - 2019: 274,330m + 1,589m - 456m = 275,463m.
  - An EU member's contribution to the EU budget is based on GNI.
- GNDI (gross national disposable income): the income available to the nation for gross saving and final consumption (CSO).
  - GNI + current transfers from the rest of the world (e.g. donations from abroad to an Irish charity) - current transfers to the rest of the world (e.g. Irish Government overseas aid) = GNDI.
  - These transfers do not include EU taxes or subsidies (already counted in GNI).
  - 2019: 275,463m - 3,609m (net) = 271,854m.
- 2018 figures: GDP 326,986m; NFYFROW -70,664m; GNP 256,322m; GNI 257,455m; GNDI 253,815m.
- Summary chain: GDP + NFYFROW = GNP; + EU subsidies - EU taxes = GNI; + current transfers in - current transfers out = GNDI.

WHICH MEASURE IS MOST ACCURATE?
- In 2019 there was a gap of close to 80bn between GDP and the other three.
- Irish GDP is not an accurate reflection of living standards. Profits of tech giants (Google, Amazon, Facebook, Apple - GAFA) are in Irish GDP but are not shared among Irish residents.
- GNP is better as a measure of economic activity related to the domestic economy alone.
- GNDI is the best indicator of living standards, as it shows money available to residents for spending and gross saving.

THE MULTIPLIER
- The multiplier effect: one person's spending is another person's income.
- Example: government gives 10m to a construction firm for a school; 6m spent on materials; 4m paid to workers in supply firms; 2m spent in local shops; 1m paid to shop workers. Total rise in national income = 10+6+4+2+1 = 23m. Multiplier = 2.3.
- MPC (marginal propensity to consume): fraction of extra income that is spent. MPC = change in C / change in Y, or MPC = 1 - MPS.
- MPS (marginal propensity to save): fraction of extra income that is saved. MPS = change in S / change in Y, or MPS = 1 - MPC.
- MPM (marginal propensity to import): fraction of extra income spent on imports. MPM = change in M / change in Y.
- MPT (marginal propensity to pay tax): fraction of extra income paid in taxes. MPT = change in T / change in Y.
- Savings = Income - Consumption. E.g. income 100 euro, spending 80 euro, savings 20 euro; MPC = 0.8, MPS = 0.2; MPC + MPS = 1.

FACTORS AFFECTING SAVINGS (and MPS)
- 1. Interest rates: high rates increase the incentive to save.
- 2. Inflation: if inflation is above the interest rate, saving falls because purchasing power is eroded. E.g. 2% interest, 3% inflation: 100 euro becomes 102 euro but the basket now costs 103 euro.
- 3. DIRT (deposit interest retention tax): a high rate discourages saving.
- 4. Incomes: rising incomes let people save more.
- 5. Expectations: optimism lowers saving; uncertainty and pessimism raise it (e.g. workers whose jobs are at risk save more).

THE MULTIPLIER FORMULAE (log tables)
- Change in national income = Injection x Multiplier.
- Example: injection 100m raises national income by 300m, so multiplier = 3.
- Worked example: target rise 500m, multiplier 2.5: injection = 500 / 2.5 = 200m.
- Closed economy with no government sector: Multiplier = 1 / MPS = 1 / (1 - MPC).
  - Closed economy: one that does not trade internationally (e.g. North Korea, which most nations do not trade with).
  - Worked example: MPC 0.6, injection 5m: 5m x 1/0.4 = 12.5m.
- Open economy with no government sector: Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM), also written 1 / ((1 - MPC) + MPM).
  - Open economy: relies heavily on international trade, e.g. Ireland.
  - Worked example: MPM 0.3, MPS 0.2, injection 10m: 10m x 1/0.5 = 10m x 2 = 20m.
- Open economy with government sector: Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM + MPT), also written 1 / ((1 - MPC) + MPM + MPT).
  - Worked example: MPM 0.4, MPT 0.24, MPS 0.26: 1 / 0.9 = 1.11.
- Full employment example: national income 100bn, full employment level 150bn, multiplier 1.25. Needed rise = 50bn. Injection = 50 / 1.25 = 40bn.

THE BUSINESS CYCLE
- Developed economies show a boom-bust pattern: sustained growth, then decline, then growth again.
- Ireland: Celtic Tiger high growth from the late 1990s to 2007; financial crash and downturn to 2012/2013; recovery until Covid-19 (2020-2021) caused another contraction.
- Figure 11.3 (CSO): GDP at constant market prices 1995-2019 rises steadily to 2007, falls in 2008, is flat/low around 2011-2013 (after the IMF/EU bailout signed at the end of 2010), then jumps between 2014 and 2015.
- John Maynard Keynes called it 'the trade cycle' (The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, 1936). He said forces pushing the economy one way first build up, then lose strength and are replaced by forces in the opposite direction.
- Diagram in words (Figure 11.4): real GDP on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal. A wavy line moves around a rising trend line: expansion up to a peak, contraction down to a trough, then expansion again.

PHASE 1: EXPANSION
- High economic growth (rising national income).
- Low interest rates encourage borrowing, discourage saving, raise investment and consumption.
- Optimistic consumers and investors.
- Ireland: Celtic Tiger (late 1990s-2007) and 2012-2019 after the Great Recession.

PHASE 2: PEAK
- The economy overheats: it reaches maximum capacity.
- Firms struggle to increase supply or recruit because of full employment.
- Inflation is high.
- Asset bubbles can form. Asset bubble: the price of an asset rises a lot in a short time without the fundamentals to justify it, e.g. the Celtic Tiger property bubble.
- Keynes: a rise in interest rates or a fall in the marginal efficiency of capital can cause the turning point.
- Example: in 2007 rising US interest rates caused the sub-prime mortgage market to collapse; sub-prime borrowers (poor credit ratings) defaulted, starting the global financial crisis.

PHASE 3: CONTRACTION/RECESSION
- Recession = a fall in GDP over two successive quarters.
- Keynes called the start 'the crisis': the turn downward is often sudden and violent; the turn upward usually is not sharp.
- Negative expectations matter, and expectations can change suddenly and violently.
- National income falls as investment and consumer spending fall; unemployment rises.
- Credit becomes less available and/or dearer; expected marginal efficiency of capital falls so investment falls.
- Pessimism keeps the downward spiral going. Inflation falls.
- Ireland 2007/8-2012: high unemployment, low consumer spending, banks reluctant to lend.

PHASE 4: TROUGH
- The lowest point. Hard to identify in real time; easier in hindsight. Features similar to contraction, but it is the turning point.

RECOVERY (RETURN TO EXPANSION)
- Keynes: low interest rates help recovery by cutting the cost of borrowing, encouraging investment and spending.
- Confidence/optimism is key.
- Ireland's recovery from 2012/13 came partly from rising confidence with strong export growth, rising FDI and more credit.

rows.prompt: What is national income?
options: The total value of all money held in a country's banks at the end of the year
The total amount of tax collected by the government over one financial year
The value of all exports sold by a country's firms to foreign buyers in a year
Income going to a country's permanent residents from current economic activity in a period
rows.explanation: National income is the income accruing to permanent residents from current economic activity, usually over one year.

rows.prompt: How is a recession defined in this chapter?
options: A fall in GDP in two successive quarters
A fall in GDP in one single quarter
A rise in unemployment for two successive months
A fall in exports over two successive years
rows.explanation: A recession is a fall in GDP in two successive quarters (two three-month periods).

rows.prompt: In the circular flow of income, what do households supply to firms?
options: Finished goods and services for sale
Factors of production, such as labour
rows.explanation: Households supply factors of production (e.g. labour) and firms pay them incomes such as wages.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an INJECTION into the circular flow?
rows.explanation: Injections are government expenditure, investment and exports; savings, taxes and imports are leakages.

rows.prompt: If injections are greater than leakages, what happens to national income?
rows.explanation: Injections add to national income and leakages reduce it, so larger injections make national income rise.

rows.prompt: Why are transfer payments NOT included in the income method?
options: They are already counted as part of exports
They are paid only once every few years
They are taxed at a rate of one hundred per cent
No factor of production has been supplied in return for them
rows.explanation: Transfer payments, e.g. child benefit, are payments for which no factor of production was supplied.

rows.prompt: A farmer sells potatoes to a restaurant for €200. The restaurant sells chips made from them for €500. What is the value of output?
rows.explanation: Counting €700 would be double counting; output is the farmer's €200 plus €300 value added = €500.

rows.prompt: Using Y = C + I + G + (X - M), calculate Y if C = €2,500m, I = €500m, G = €600m, X = €300m and M = €200m.
Which change would most likely REDUCE consumer spending?
options: A cut in direct taxes on labour
rows.explanation: Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, so consumer spending falls.

rows.prompt: Under the EU rules mentioned in the chapter, what is the limit on a member state's budget deficit?
rows.explanation: The deficit should not exceed 3% of GDP and public debt should be under 60% of GDP.

rows.prompt: The exchange rate moves from €1 = $1.20 to €1 = $1.10. What is the likely effect on Irish exports to the US?
options: They fall, because Irish goods become dearer for Americans
They rise, because US incomes automatically increase
They fall, because the euro has become stronger
They rise, because Irish goods become cheaper for Americans
rows.explanation: A fall in the value of the euro makes Irish exports more attractive outside the eurozone.

rows.prompt: Country A has debt of €90bn and GDP of €100bn. What is its debt/GDP ratio?
rows.explanation: 90 divided by 100 = 90%.

rows.prompt: What is the difference between nominal GDP and real GDP?
options: Nominal uses constant prices; real uses current prices
Nominal includes exports; real excludes exports
Nominal uses current prices; real uses constant prices
Nominal is per person; real is for the whole country
rows.explanation: Real GDP removes the effect of inflation/deflation by valuing output at constant prices.

rows.prompt: GDP doubles from €10bn to €20bn while population doubles from 1m to 2m. GDP per capita is:
Which of these is part of the hidden (shadow) economy?
rows.explanation: The hidden economy includes unrecorded activity such as drug dealing, fuel laundering and cigarette smuggling.

rows.prompt: Which type of intellectual property protects creative works such as books and music?
rows.explanation: Copyright applies to creative works, e.g. books, music and films.

rows.prompt: In the Tasty Cakes example, why is the IP registered to the Irish HQ?
options: To qualify for EU subsidies paid to Irish firms
To avoid paying any VAT on cake sales in France
To pay Ireland's lower corporation tax rate on most of its income
To make the French subsidiary more profitable
rows.explanation: Registering IP in Ireland lets the firm pay the lower Irish corporation tax rate (12.5%) instead of the French rate.

rows.prompt: GDP measures goods and services produced by:
options: Irish-owned factors in Ireland and abroad
Irish- and foreign-owned factors in the domestic economy only
rows.explanation: GDP covers all production inside the domestic economy, whoever owns the factors.

rows.prompt: Why is net factor income from the rest of the world negative for Ireland?
options: Irish emigrants send home more money than foreign workers send abroad
EU taxes paid by Ireland are larger than EU subsidies received
Income sent abroad by foreign factors in Ireland exceeds income sent home by Irish factors abroad
Ireland imports more goods and services than it exports
rows.explanation: More foreign MNC profits, immigrant remittances and interest go out than come in.

rows.prompt: GDP is €100m and net factor income from the rest of the world is -€20m. What is GNP?
rows.explanation: GNP = GDP + NFYFROW = 100 + (-20) = €80m.

rows.prompt: Which was a reason for the 26% surge in Irish GDP in 2015?
options: Inversion deals such as the Medtronic and Covidien merger
A large rise in the number of Irish emigrants
A sharp rise in EU subsidies to farmers
A big increase in public sector salaries
rows.explanation: Inversion deals, IP relocation and aircraft leasing assets inflated 2015 GDP.

rows.prompt: GNP is €80m, EU subsidies are €8m and EU taxes are €10m. What is GNI?
rows.explanation: GNI = GNP + EU subsidies - EU taxes = 80 + 8 - 10 = €78m.

rows.prompt: Which measure is the best indicator of the living standards of Irish residents?
rows.explanation: GNDI shows the money available to residents for consumption and gross saving.

rows.prompt: If MPC is 0.8, what is MPS?
In a closed economy with no government, MPC = 0.6. What rise in national income results from a €5m injection?
In an open economy, MPS = 0.2 and MPM = 0.3 (no government sector). What is the multiplier?
rows.explanation: Multiplier = 1/(MPS + MPM) = 1/0.5 = 2.

rows.prompt: National income is €100bn, the full employment level is €150bn and the multiplier is 1.25. What injection is needed?
rows.explanation: Needed rise is €50bn; injection = 50 / 1.25 = €40bn.

rows.prompt: Interest rates are 2% and inflation is 3%. What happens to the incentive to save?
options: It rises, as savings earn more interest
It falls, as savings lose purchasing power
It is unaffected, as both rates are low
It rises, as prices are expected to fall
rows.explanation: When inflation is above the interest rate, the purchasing power of savings is eroded, so saving falls.

rows.prompt: Which phase of the business cycle is the lowest point of the downturn?
rows.explanation: The trough is the lowest point of the downward movement and is a turning point.

rows.prompt: Which feature is typical of the PEAK phase?
options: High inflation and firms struggling to recruit
Banks reluctant to lend and falling GDP
rows.explanation: At the peak the economy overheats: full employment, high inflation, possible asset bubbles.

rows.prompt: According to Keynes, what can cause the turning point at the peak?
options: A fall in interest rates or a rise in consumer confidence
A rise in exports or a rise in government spending
A fall in inflation or a rise in savings incentives
A rise in interest rates or a fall in the marginal efficiency of capital
rows.explanation: Keynes suggested rising interest rates or a falling marginal efficiency of capital could cause the turn.

rows.prompt: Describe in words a diagram of the circular flow of income in an open economy with a government.
rows.model_answer: Households supply factors of production to firms and receive incomes; households spend on firms' output. Leakages leave the flow: taxes to the government, savings to financial institutions and imports to foreign markets. Injections return: government expenditure, investment and exports. If injections exceed leakages national income rises; if less, it falls.

rows.prompt: Name the three methods of measuring national income and explain one in your own words.
rows.model_answer: The expenditure method, the output method and the income method. The output method adds the output of all firms, avoiding double counting by not including intermediate goods - e.g. potatoes sold for €200 and turned into €500 of chips count as €500, not €700.

rows.prompt: Give three reasons why national income statistics are calculated.
rows.model_answer: They measure economic growth over time. They help with economic planning, e.g. checking if a tax cut increased national income. They show changes in the standard of living, and they are used for the debt/GDP ratio and for working out the EU budget contribution (based on GNI).

rows.prompt: Explain three limitations of national income statistics.
rows.model_answer: They do not show population changes, so GDP per capita may be unchanged. Rises can be due to inflation rather than more output, so real GDP at constant prices is used. They ignore unpaid work like GAA volunteers, ignore the hidden economy, and say nothing about how income is distributed or about wellbeing such as longer commutes.

rows.prompt: Name two effects of the hidden economy and two ways the government could reduce it.
rows.model_answer: Legitimate retailers lose sales and profits, and the government loses VAT and excise revenue. The government could bring in harsher fines and prison sentences, or lower indirect taxes and taxes on labour so there is less incentive to buy or work in the hidden economy.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between GDP and GNP and say which is bigger in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: GDP measures output by Irish- and foreign-owned factors in the domestic economy only; GNP measures output by Irish-owned factors at home and abroad. GDP plus net factor income from the rest of the world equals GNP. In Ireland GDP is bigger because net factor income is negative - foreign MNCs repatriate large profits.

rows.prompt: Explain how you get from GNP to GNI, and from GNI to GNDI.
rows.model_answer: GNI = GNP plus EU subsidies minus EU taxes. GNDI = GNI plus current transfers from the rest of the world (e.g. donations to an Irish charity) minus current transfers to the rest of the world (e.g. Irish overseas aid). GNDI shows income available for gross saving and consumption.

rows.prompt: State three factors that affect the level of savings in an economy.
rows.model_answer: Interest rates - higher rates increase the incentive to save. Inflation - if it is higher than the interest rate, saving falls as purchasing power is eroded. DIRT - a high rate discourages saving. Incomes and expectations also matter; pessimism makes people save more.

rows.prompt: Name the four phases of the business cycle and describe the business cycle diagram in words.
rows.model_answer: Expansion, peak, contraction (recession) and trough. The diagram has real GDP on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal; a wavy line rises to a peak, falls to a trough and rises again, moving around an upward-sloping trend line.

rows.prompt: (a) Distinguish between GDP and GNP. (b) Explain why GDP is not an accurate measure of living standards in Ireland, and state which measure is better. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) GDP measures the value of goods and services produced by Irish- and foreign-owned factors of production in the domestic economy only. GNP measures the value produced by Irish-owned factors at home and abroad. GDP plus net factor income from the rest of the world equals GNP; in Ireland this figure is negative, e.g. in 2019 GDP was €356,051m and GNP €274,330m. (b) Ireland's GDP is inflated by multinationals. The profits of tech giants such as Google, Amazon, Facebook and Apple are counted in GDP but are repatriated, not shared among Irish residents. MNCs have moved intellectual property to Ireland to pay the 12.5% corporation tax rate, so foreign earnings are recorded here. Inversion deals, like Medtronic merging with Covidien, and aircraft leasing firms moving assets here caused a 26% jump in GDP in 2015 that did not reflect real living standards. In 2019 the gap between GDP and the other measures was close to €80bn. GNDI is the best measure of living standards, as it shows the money residents have for consumption and gross saving; GNP is better for domestic economic activity.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) GDP defined 5m (2+3), GNP defined 5m (2+3). (b) 3 points x 4m (2m statement + 2m explanation) e.g. MNC profits repatriated; IP relocation; inversion deals / aircraft leasing / 2015 surge; better measure named and explained (GNDI or GNP) 3m.

rows.prompt: MPC = 0.8 and MPM = 0.2. Current national income is €500m and the full employment level is €620m. (i) Calculate the MPS. (ii) Calculate the multiplier for this open economy (no government sector). (iii) Calculate the injection needed to reach full employment. Show all workings. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) MPS = 1 - MPC = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. (ii) Multiplier = 1 / (MPS + MPM) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5. (iii) Required rise in national income = €620m - €500m = €120m. Change in national income = injection x multiplier, so injection = €120m / 2.5 = €48m.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 4m: formula 2m, answer 2m. (ii) 5m: correct formula 2m, workings 1m, answer 2m. (iii) 6m: gap of €120m 2m, method 2m, answer €48m 2m.

rows.prompt: Discuss the economic effects of the hidden (shadow) economy and outline measures the government could take to reduce its size. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The hidden economy is unrecorded activity not in national income statistics, e.g. the drugs trade, fuel laundering, cigarette smuggling and cash work without tax returns. Effects: legitimate retailers lose sales and profits, e.g. a shop selling cigarettes at €14 cannot compete with a smuggler at €5. Unemployment can rise as legitimate firms lose business, cutting tax revenue and raising jobseeker's allowance costs. VAT and excise duties go uncollected, leaving less for government spending. The state must spend scarce resources on customs, Gardaí and prisons, with an opportunity cost such as less community policing. Counterfeit goods are not made to safety rules and may harm health. Measures: harsher fines and prison sentences; more resources for Gardaí and customs; awareness campaigns; lower indirect taxes to remove the incentive to buy illegally; lower taxes on labour so people do not work for cash to avoid USC, PAYE and PRSI.
rows.marking_scheme: Effects: 3 points x 4m (2m statement + 2m explanation) = 12m. Measures: 2 points x 4m (2m + 2m) = 8m.

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the four phases of the business cycle, referring to the Irish economy. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram: real GDP on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal; a wavy line rises and falls around an upward trend line, labelled expansion, peak, contraction and trough. Expansion: high growth in national income, low interest rates encouraging investment and spending, optimistic consumers and investors, e.g. the Celtic Tiger from the late 1990s to 2007 and 2012-2019. Peak: the economy overheats at maximum capacity; firms struggle to recruit due to full employment, inflation is high and asset bubbles form, e.g. the Irish property bubble. Keynes said rising interest rates or a falling marginal efficiency of capital can cause the turn, e.g. the 2007 US sub-prime collapse. Contraction: GDP falls for two successive quarters (recession); investment and spending fall, unemployment rises, credit is scarce and pessimism spreads; inflation falls, e.g. Ireland 2007/8-2012. Trough: the lowest point and the turning point, hard to see in real time. Recovery comes from low interest rates and returning confidence, e.g. rising exports, FDI and credit from 2012/13.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram correctly labelled 5m. 4 phases x 5m (2m feature statement + 2m explanation + 1m Irish example) = 20m.
